extracted.intended_audience: CRTC commissioners, CRTC staff, regulated broadcasters and telecommunications carriers, policy-makers and stakeholders in Canadian broadcasting/telecommunications regulation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and recommendations on CRTC procedures covering confidentiality, public access to materials, complaints handling, hearing formats, panel decision-making, and organizational specialization for broadcasting and telecommunications regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality test for broadcasting applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Before information will be treated as confidential in broadcasting applications, the applicant must establish to the satisfaction of the Commission that disclosure will cause specific direct harm that outweighs the benefit to be derived from public disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission proposes to apply the test evolved in its telecommunications proceedings to broadcasting applications. The applicant bears the burden of establishing specific direct harm; disclosure is denied only where such harm is shown to outweigh public benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory confidentiality standard in telecommunications (Sections 331 and 334)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sections in the Railway Act (e.g., s.331 and s.334) provide that certain information obtained from carriers (costs or other confidential information) shall not be published or revealed unless, in the opinion of the Commission, publication is necessary in the public interest or there appear to be 'good and sufficient reasons' for release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These provisions were intended to provide confidentiality for carrier costs; disclosure is the exception rather than the rule under the statute. The Commission has had to interpret and balance these statutory protections against the needs of public hearings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden-shifting in confidentiality disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: Where interveners need relevant information to assist them, the onus shifts to the carriers to prove that disclosure would cause specific direct harm; interveners need only state their need for the information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice the Commission required disclosure of most of an economic study in a case unless specific direct harm were proven by the carrier. This approach effectively reversed the onus implicit in the statutory text and has made it difficult for carriers to meet the test because competitive harm is often speculative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of Commission staff briefing notes and staff documents
rubrics_metrics.description: All material prepared by Commission staff prior to hearings (briefing notes, summaries of application material, background studies) should be made public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Staff documents prepared for the assistance of sitting Commissioners should be made public because they enhance the quality of participation; applicants and interveners may benefit from knowing contents in advance and commenting on them in oral presentations. Warning: summaries/briefs may mis-state or prejudice an applicant's case, so transparency permits correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public file and regular reporting requirement for licensees/carriers
rubrics_metrics.description: Information about licensees and carriers should be available on a continuous basis via public files at licensee offices and by making monthly or quarterly reports currently filed confidentially available to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission suggested access to regular reports and confirmed benefits from publishing statistical reports on carrier activities. The public file for broadcasting and reports for telecommunications help effective public participation and research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telecommunications Bulletin and equivalent broadcasting bulletin
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a regular bulletin (telecommunications bulletin exists) and prepare a similar monthly broadcasting bulletin summarizing important developments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Telecommunications Bulletin is divided into three parts: (1) status report on active proceedings (continuously updated); (2) summaries of recent decisions and orders of general interest; (3) chronological table of orders made during the period. A broadcasting bulletin would help track voluminous broadcasting announcements, especially since the Commission discontinued circulating full decisions/announcements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessible record and subject-matter index of past decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a practical system for making the record of previous proceedings available and maintain a current index to subject matter of broadcasting decisions (not merely organized by locality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An index (included in the proposed monthly bulletin) would allow researching decisions by subject; the current annual bound volume organized by locality is inadequate for subject-based research. Re-institute annual reports that summarize major decisions under subject headings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complaints handling model (telecommunications style) for broadcasting
rubrics_metrics.description: Appoint dedicated full‑time complaints officers on the broadcasting side whose sole responsibility is to deal with all incoming complaints and to provide prompt, consistent, and activist resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Telecommunications complaints are handled effectively by two full-time staff who require companies to respond directly, assess justification, initiate and follow-up action, visit undertakings or meet parties when necessary. Broadcasting complaints are currently dispersed and often not followed up; adopting the telecom model would improve timeliness and consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope principle: do not act as censor; defer to courts where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission's function is not to act as a censor of programs; complaints involving libel, obscenity or other matters for which there is recourse to the courts should be resolved in the courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broadcasting complaints often raise individual standards or questions of taste which the Commission considers outside regulatory purview; for issues involving legal remedies (e.g., libel), the courts are the appropriate forum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain two distinct procedural characters (broadcasting informal; telecommunications formal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Continue to use both the broadcasting hearing format (more informal, public dialogue) and the telecommunications formal procedures (court-like, rigorous testing of technical/economic evidence), because each suits the character and regulatory objectives of its area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each set of procedures should be preserved though elements of one may be used in the other when appropriate (e.g., broadcasting format for policy hearings; limited cross-examination in broadcasting where adversarial positions are strong). Full-time members' experience with formal procedures can inform more vigorous questioning in broadcasting hearings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel that hears should decide the matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Decision-making should be aligned with the hearing panel: the panel which hears a matter should decide it rather than broader collegial decision-making detached from the hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collegial decision-making can produce procedural injustices and practical difficulties in complex technical proceedings because members who did not participate in the hearing may lack sufficient knowledge to make informed decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialization of Commissioners by regulatory area
rubrics_metrics.description: Allocate most Commissioners to either telecommunications or broadcasting and have them spend their full time in the designated area to gain requisite expertise (economics/accounting/technology for telecom; cultural/software emphasis for broadcasting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specialization improves ability to follow developments domestically and abroad, develop creative regulatory solutions, and strengthen confidence of regulated companies and the public. Cross-over concerns should be managed by joint panels and Executive Committee meetings; the Chairman should provide neutral policy overview and liaison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase out part‑time Commissioners as expertise needs grow
rubrics_metrics.description: Because major broadcasting and telecommunications issues demand full‑time depth of knowledge, the position of part‑time Commissioners should be phased out as terms expire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part-time members historically represented local/sectoral interests, but regional offices, public interest groups, and frequent public hearings now provide mechanisms for regional input. The regulatory load and complexity make full‑time specialization more appropriate; part‑time members have become less significant since exclusion from telecommunications regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency principle to enhance quality of public participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Effectiveness of regulatory process depends on quality of intervener participation; interveners must, in principle, have as much relevant information as possible to discharge their role, subject to demonstrable risk of specific direct harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle underlies recommendations for greater disclosure (staff documents, summaries, public files, bulletins) and explains why statutory confidentiality protections have been narrowly interpreted by the Commission in favor of disclosure unless harm is proven.
